query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: We hypothesize that, in Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloys, local compositional fluctuations lead to regionally varying stacking-fault energies that promote dislocation cross-slip and short-range ordering, enhancing both strength and ductility over a wide range of temperatures and strain rates. This synergy underlies the alloy’s improved dynamic performance compared to conventional Co-containing systems.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-solution-annealed Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy with a single-phase FCC microstructure.
generation.intervention: In-situ high-strain-rate mechanical testing combined with microstructure characterization and complementary simulation.
generation.conditions: Temperatures spanning cryogenic to elevated (~77 K to ~800 K) and strain rates from 10^(-3) s^(-1) to 10^3 s^(-1).
generation.structural_mediator: Dislocation cross-slip and localized short-range ordering stimulated by moderate stacking-fault energy variations.
generation.mechanism: Inhomogeneous local ordering and partial dislocation motion become more pronounced as temperature or strain rate increases, promoting dynamic slip and forest hardening mechanisms that stabilize plastic flow and delay fracture, thereby achieving a favorable strength–ductility balance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline at similar test conditions, the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy exhibits greater strain-rate sensitivity and displays enhanced strain-hardening and ductility at intermediate temperatures, leading to extended uniform deformation and higher energy absorption before failure.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi tested in the same temperature and strain-rate window to isolate the role of cobalt removal and the resultant dislocation processes.
generation.boundary: For temperatures below ~77 K or beyond ~800 K, or for strain rates outside 10^(-3)–10^3 s^(-1), dominant deformation modes may shift (e.g., phase transformations, extensive dynamic recovery), limiting the proposed mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contribution of short-range ordering to the alloy’s rate sensitivity is not fully confirmed, requiring further targeted high-resolution characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform head-to-head, in-situ high-strain-rate compression (or tension) tests on Co-free FeNiCrMn and CoCrFeMnNi at temperatures from ~77 K to ~800 K and strain rates from 10^(-3) s^(-1) to 10^3 s^(-1), coupled with real-time synchrotron or neutron diffraction to track microstructural changes.
measurements: Stress–strain curves across tested strain rates and temperatures
Evolving dislocation density and twin fraction from in-situ diffraction data
Post-mortem electron microscopy (TEM/EBSD) for dislocation structures, short-range ordering, and twinning
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy shows no enhanced strain-rate–temperature response or microstructure evolution distinct from the CoCrFeMnNi baseline, then the hypothesized role of local compositional fluctuations and short-range ordering in modulating dynamic strength–ductility is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: At temperatures above 650 °C, no serrations are observed prior to the critical failure (see Table 1).Increasing the number of sources and the size differences of various atomic pairs (the atomic radii in FCC structures are: RNi = 1.25 Å, RCo = 1.25 Å, RFe = 1.27 Å, RCr = 1.28 Å, and RMn = 1.26 Å) in the lattice causes a lower and wider temperature range in which serration behavior is observed (and in which the healing rate, Λ, increases and decreases again with temperature). This trend explains why the quinary alloy has the largest range, while the ternary alloy has the narrowest range. Ni and CoNi alloys are lacking sufficient sources and size differences and, accordingly, show no PLC effect (see Table 1).Lowering the strain-rate can decrease the high-temperature limit of the serration behavior because lower strain-rates allow atoms to have more time to successfully lock the dislocations. Table 2 demonstrates this effect. A strain-rate of 1 × 10−5/s produces serration behavior at 300 °C, whereas a strain-rate of 1 × 10−4/s does not.The PLC effect of CoCrFeMnNi remains at higher strain-rates up to 10−2/s for higher temperatures except for 300 °C.

The fracture strain of Cantor alloy is strongly affected by the strain rate within the range 10−3 to 10 s−1 at high temperatures (), while its yield strength is insensitive to the strain rate at different temperatures (, ). Low temperature is found beneficial to the strain hardening of CrMnFeCoNi (), and annealing-induced abnormal hardening is observed after cold work, which is attributed to the long-range ordered structure (). Because of their superior mechanical properties, especially the excellent strain hardening ability, the HEAs have great potential to be used for ballistic protection. However, there are very limited reports regarding the application or potential application of HEAs in ballistic protection (). Both dislocations and deformation TW were observed near bullet holes on HEAs and were considered responsible for their antiballistic performance (, ). However, in situ observations of dynamic response of the HEAs to ballistic impact are in lack or very limited for further fundamental understanding, and the influence of chemical composition to the alloys’ ballistic performance is not included in the experimental studies.
